prize_parts.citation: For the chemistry of ionizable lipid nanoparticles that enables the delivery of nucleic-acid medicines

statement.case_for: Ionizable lipid nanoparticles are a molecular design solution to a concrete chemical problem: how to package, protect and release a polyanionic nucleic acid inside a cell. pKa-tuned ionizable lipids are neutral in blood and charged in the endosome, driving membrane destabilisation and release; this, together with controlled self-assembly and encapsulation, is physical and synthetic chemistry. The consequence is unusually direct, since the same platform carries siRNA therapy (patisiran) and mRNA vaccines at global scale. Independent validation is as strong as it gets for any shortlisted candidate. The 2023 Medicine prize honoured the nucleoside modification of the cargo; the vehicle that makes the cargo work is the chemistry half of the same story. After reading colleagues' arguments I tighten the trio to Cullis (foundational ionizable-lipid and LNP principles), Hope (encapsulation and size-control methods, with Madden at the origin of the Vancouver platform) and Anderson (combinatorial lipidoid design that opened the modern ionizable-lipid chemical space). I moved MacLachlan out of my trio because two colleagues credit the Vancouver core as the decisive origin and the clinical translation, while important, is more a development than an invention.
statement.case_against: Attribution is the real weakness: Madden, MacLachlan and Langer are all substantial contributors who a three-person limit forces out, and patent and priority disputes around specific lipids may make any trio look arbitrary. There is also a fair argument that this is pharmaceutical formulation rather than a discovery in chemistry, and that after the 2023 Medicine prize the urgency is lower. If the committee cannot defend a trio, B009 or B008 may be cleaner.

responses.point: PROTACs and molecular glues are a genuinely new pharmacological modality, with the Crews/Deshaies/Sakamoto proof of principle and Handa and Ito's cereblon mechanism as the decisive steps.
responses.response: I agree this is a new modality and ranked it second. My reservation is timing and attribution: no degrader is approved, so the clinical payoff the case rests on is still promised rather than delivered, and omitting Ciulli, Gray and Sakamoto is a serious problem for a concept-plus-mechanism trio. Lipid nanoparticles have already delivered approved medicines. I would not oppose B009 as a later prize, but I would not choose it ahead of B016 this year.

responses.point: Base editing turns a defined deaminase reaction into a programmable tool, with Liu, Komor and Gaudelli as a clean trio, and ranks B016 third with the Vancouver trio Cullis, Madden and Hope.
responses.response: I accept the clean attribution for B008 and the mechanistic clarity, and I credit your point that the Vancouver group is the core of B016, which I adopted by moving Hope into my trio. However, base editing follows the 2020 genome-editing prize and its long-term clinical safety is not yet known, so I see it as a strong alternative but not the first choice. I disagree that the 2023 Medicine prize reduces the case for B016: that prize addressed the cargo, not the delivery chemistry.

responses.point: Lipid self-assembly and ionizable-lipid design is physical chemistry with enormous societal impact, with a Cullis/Hope/MacLachlan configuration, while B003 phase separation is ranked first.
responses.response: We agree on the Vancouver origin, and your pKa-dependent charge and bilayer-to-non-bilayer phase behaviour is exactly the physical-chemical framing I would want in the citation. I part ways on B003: you yourself note that physiological relevance versus in vitro droplets is still debated, and a prize needs a settled core. Where I would push back on your trio is that leaving out Anderson drops the lipidoid chemistry that broadened the field beyond a single lipid family.

responses.point: Pd-catalysed C-N coupling is conceptually clear, pervasive in medicinal and process chemistry, and recognition is overdue, with Buchwald and Hartwig as the right pair.
responses.response: The synthetic case is strong and attribution is cleaner than for B016, so I take your point seriously. My difficulty is comparative: the 2010 cross-coupling prize already rewarded the central logic of Pd catalysis, whereas lipid nanoparticles open a field no prize has recognised. I agree Kosugi should not take a place. I would see B011 as the safest consensus fallback if the committee cannot agree on lipid credit.

uncertainties: Whether the committee accepts delivery formulation as a chemistry discovery rather than pharmaceutical development
Fair allocation among Cullis, Hope, Madden, MacLachlan, Anderson and Langer, and the effect of patent disputes
Whether the 2023 Medicine prize makes a closely related Chemistry prize look redundant
Whether B009 will be mature enough in a year or two to overtake B016 on clinical validation
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from my profile. I have no recorded tie to the Vancouver, Alnylam or MIT groups; my only overlap is topical, with Emma Sparr's work on lipid and peptide self-assembly, and my own nanoparticle and peptide work does not involve any candidate.
